title: memory-fragmentation-oom-root-cause-notes-v3
content:
Purpose:
We were seeing intermittent OOMs on production Dedicated hosts (p3/4-equivalent nodes) even though nvidia-smi reported a sizeable amount of free memory. This doc captures the investigation of GPU memory fragmentation and allocator behavior that led to the OOMs and lists short/medium/long-term mitigations and reproducible checks.

Symptoms observed:
- Intermittent OOMs during high-concurrency inference workloads (mixed short and long sequences).
- OOMs correlated with short traffic bursts rather than sustained high throughput.
- nvidia-smi showed ~2-4 GB free at the time of failure, yet cudaMalloc failed for ~1-2 GB requests.
- Problems more frequent after a period of varied request sizes and several model reloads.

Environment and tooling used:
- Serving runtime: internal inference engine v2.8.x (C++ allocator + per-request workspaces).
- CUDA 11.7 driver stack on AWS instances with heterogeneous GPU types.
- Tracing tools: Nsight Systems for timeline, NVML (python bindings) for free/used memory polling, LD_PRELOAD interceptor to log cudaMalloc/cudaFree traces, and custom allocator logging hooks.
- Reproducer harness: a python script that fires mixed-size requests to the local runtime and logs all cudaMalloc/cudaFree sizes/timestamps.

Reproduction steps (short):
1) Start local serving-runtime with debug allocator logging enabled (ALLOC_LOG=1).
2) Run the reproducer that issues 90% small requests (short seq/batch) and 10% large requests (long seq) concurrently with concurrency=8.
3) Observe sequence of allocations and frees; watch for large allocation failures despite aggregate free memory.
4) Capture timeline in Nsight to correlate kernels with allocation attempts.

Key observations from traces:
- The allocator maintained many small free blocks scattered across device memory after long-running traffic with variable sizes.
- Large workspace allocations (for long sequences / large batch) failed even when total free memory > request size. The failure coincided with scatter of free blocks too small to satisfy the contiguous allocation.
- Frequent cudaMalloc/cudaFree pairs from transient buffers (per-request temporary tensors, cuBLAS/cuDNN workspace) caused fragmentation.
- The default device allocator in the runtime does not coalesce adjacent free blocks aggressively.
- Some libraries (cuBLASLt / cuDNN) request transient workspaces of variable size per-kernel; these can be large and non-deterministic depending on algorithm choice.

Root-cause analysis:
1) Mixed allocation patterns: interleaving many small ephemeral allocations with occasional large workspace requests created a fragmented free-space map.
2) No global pooling for large workspaces: large allocations went to cudaMalloc / cudaFree and relied on the OS-level allocator behavior rather than a persistent pool, increasing fragmentation risk.
3) Allocator metadata placement and lack of coalescing: our allocator metadata layout and free-list policy prevented efficient merging of adjacent free blocks, so small freed blocks stayed unusable for larger requests.
4) Library workspace behavior: cuBLAS/cuDNN sometimes select algorithms that need large temporary buffers at runtime. When those buffers could not be allocated contiguously, the library returned an error that surfaced as OOM.
5) Model reloads and dynamic quantization paths: model load/unload cycles further scattered allocations (some pinned allocations persisted), increasing fragmentation over time.

Evidence supporting root causes:
- LD_PRELOAD traces showed sequence: many small frees followed by a large cudaMalloc that failed.
- Nsight timeline confirmed that large kernel launches were preceded by allocation attempts and OOMs.
- Reproducer: after running mixed traffic for ~10 minutes, the number of free blocks increased while the maximum contiguous free block decreased.

Immediate mitigations (short-term):
- Avoid calling cudaFree for per-request ephemeral objects in hot path where possible; instead reuse buffers from a small cache. Implement a short-lived per-thread buffer pool.
- Configure the inference engine to prefer algorithms with smaller workspace requirements (when available) under memory pressure (algorithm heuristics).
- Add conservative per-model workspace caps so a single request cannot request the entire heap. Return 429 / degrade instead of attempting huge allocations.
- Enable cudaMallocAsync (if runtime CUDA >= 11.2 and supported on instance) in experimental builds to take advantage of async caching allocator behavior. Note: validate correctness; cudaMallocAsync has different semantics for streaming.
- Increase logging around allocator failures to capture requested sizes and fragmentation metrics when an OOM happens.

Medium-term fixes (next 1-2 sprints):
- Implement a hybrid allocator: small allocations handled by existing caching allocator; large workspace allocations routed to a reserved large-block pool with coalescing and best-fit placement.
- Add an explicit workspace reservation phase per request: before compute kernels run, try to reserve required workspace from the pool; if reservation fails, fall back to cheaper algorithm or queue the request.
- Integrate allocator tracing into CI benchmarks to catch fragmentation regressions (generate allocation/free heatmaps during load tests).
- Add logic to pin and occasionally compact long-lived blocks (where possible) to reduce scatter - for example keep model parameter allocations separate from transient workspace pools.

Long-term recommendations (architecture):
- Adopt a production-grade GPU memory manager that supports defragmentation strategies and fast coalescing, or upstream improvements to the existing caching allocator semantics.
- Work with framework/library teams to control workspace sizes (e.g., expose deterministic workspace selection or let client pass preferred algorithm to avoid surprising large allocations).
- Consider reserving a small fragmentation buffer (safety headroom) that can be used for opportunistic compaction or to satisfy single large allocations without triggering OOM.

Validation and benchmarks after fixes (examples):
- Reproducer baseline: under mixed traffic, we saw OOMs ~6-12/hour. After short-term fixes (buffer reuse + algorithm selection) OOMs dropped to 0 in 24h stress run for the same load profile.
- Memory fragmentation metric: maximum contiguous free block increased by ~30-50% after switching large workloads to the reserved pool in synthetic benchmarks (measured via allocator trace).
- Tail-latency: small regression in tail latency for some requests when preferring smaller-workspace algorithms; traded off for higher availability.

Operational checks to add to observability (should be instrumented):
- Track fragmentation metrics: total free memory, number of free blocks, largest free block, fragmentation ratio (= 1 - largest_free_block / total_free).
- Log allocation failures with requested size, largest_free_block_at_failure, backtrace of allocation site.
- Emit per-model/workload workspace histogram to determine common sizes and tune pool sizes.
- Health rule: alert when fragmentation ratio > 0.7 for >5 minutes and concurrent large allocation attempts observed.

Reproducers and scripts (pointer):
- reproducer/mixed_alloc_repro.py - fires mixed-size requests with configurable ratios and logs allocator traces (LD_PRELOAD or runtime hook).
- tools/alloc_trace_parser.py - parses allocator logs into a time-series and computes fragmentation stats.
- CI job: perf/fragmentation-smoke that runs small reproducer and asserts fragmentation ratio < 0.6.

Next steps / owner action items:
- (Maya) land additional allocator debug logging behind a feature flag and run the reproducer at scale in staging.
- (Ethan) implement short-term per-thread buffer reuse for ephemeral tensors and measure improvement.
- (Ravi) prototype reserved large-block pool and run 24h stress tests.
- (Lina) add fragmentation metrics to the Console dashboard and create alert rules.

Open questions / unknowns:
- How will cudaMallocAsync behave under our mixed-size workload in production (stream interaction)? Need controlled experiment.
- Is there a workload-specific pattern we can automatically detect and optimize (e.g., if >X% of requests need large workspace, switch to a different serving partition)?
- What tradeoffs do we accept for algorithm selection (accuracy vs workspace size vs latency)?

Appendix: useful commands and traces to collect
- NVML polling (python): poll device memory free/used at 100ms granularity during reproducer.
- Nsight Systems: capture 30s window around OOM to correlate allocation attempts and kernel activity.
- LD_PRELOAD allocator logger: build a small shim to log all cudaMalloc/cudaFree with sizes + timestamps.
- nvidia-smi (sampling): nvidia-smi dmon can be useful but is too coarse for per-request diagnosis.

Summary:
Memory fragmentation was the proximate cause of OOMs: a mix of small ephemeral allocations and occasional large workspaces left the device with sufficient aggregate free memory but no large contiguous block to satisfy big allocations. Short-term mitigations (buffer reuse, algorithm tuning, conservative workspace caps) remove most observed OOMs in staging. Medium-term work is to implement a hybrid allocator with a reserved pool for large workspaces and better coalescing. Instrumentation and CI checks are critical to detect regressions early.

End of notes.
